title: The Hundred and First
subtitle: The Legend of Genkai of Kōzan
teaser: A hundred monks went down to hold the bridge at Ume with nothing in their hands. Their teacher was ordered to stay behind and keep the lamps lit, and he kept them lit for forty years.

sections.heading: I. The Fist
paragraphs: Every disciple of Kōzan carved one bead for his teacher, from the plum trees that grew along the river at Ume. Ninety-nine of them carved round beads. Isamu carved a fist.
It was the size of a pea, four knuckles and a thumb, with a hole bored through the wrist.
“It’s a bead,” he said, before Master Genkai could speak. “It has a hole in it. That’s all a bead needs.”
Genkai threaded it onto his string between two round ones. He wears it still.
Kōzan stood at the top of a hundred stone steps above the river. It kept the valley’s grain, and it kept the open hand. On the first morning, Genkai told each of his hundred disciples the same thing.
“Every man is standing on something. His feet. His sword. His anger. Take it away and he sits down. And a man who is sitting down can be talked to.”
Then he said, “Come.” When they came at him, he laid his palm flat on their chests, and they sat down.
Isamu took it as an insult. He was a charcoal burner’s son from Ume who had come up the steps at twelve with a split lip, and he argued with everything.
“And when an army comes up the road? We talk to all of them?”
“If they sit still.”
“A fist would be quicker.”
“A fist can hold one thing,” Genkai said. “An open hand can hold whatever you put in it.”
Genkai sat him down. Isamu got up arguing. They did it so often the others stopped noticing, the way you stop hearing a mill wheel.
“One day it’ll matter,” Isamu said once, from the floor, “and I’ll close my hand, and you’ll see.”
“One day it will matter,” said Genkai, “and you’ll open it. And you’ll see.”
He loved all hundred of them. Isamu was the only one who ever got up arguing, and Genkai never told him how much he looked forward to it.

sections.heading: II. The Bridge at Ume
paragraphs: In Genkai’s fortieth autumn, the warlord Oda Kurogane came over the hills with three thousand hungry men, for Kōzan’s grain. Without it, the valley would starve by spring.

The grain could be hidden in the caves above the temple, but that would take every cart in the valley a full day, and the only road crossed the bridge at Ume: black timber over deep water, four men wide.
Someone had to hold it until sunset. The hundred settled it among themselves in the time it takes to boil rice. Nobody asked Genkai.
That night the abbot lit a hundred lamps in the great hall. At Kōzan, when a disciple went down the mountain, a lamp burned for him until he came home and blew it out himself. Nobody else could.
Then the abbot turned to Genkai. “You’ll stay here. Keep the lamps lit.”
“I taught them. I should be on that bridge.”
“You taught them,” said the abbot. “If you die on that bridge, who teaches the next hundred?”
Genkai argued. It is the one argument of his life he has never been proud of, because of how quickly he let himself lose it.
At dawn, Isamu stopped in the gate.
“When I come back,” he said, “I’m blowing out my own lamp, and you’re admitting I was right.”
“About what?”
“Whatever happens. I’ll decide on the way up.”

Genkai watched all day from the temple gallery. Kurogane’s men came onto the bridge four at a time, and four at a time they went off it into the river. Nobody on the near end carried a blade. By noon the far bank was lined with soldiers wringing out their clothes.
In the afternoon the soldiers stopped coming. Genkai saw why before he let himself understand it: a line of archers, kneeling on the far bank.
Behind him, the last carts were creaking up the mountain. Below him, the grey robes went down in fours. They did not step back. Behind them was the road to Kōzan, and the carts.
The sun set. The last cart reached the caves. The bridge was quiet.
Genkai trimmed a hundred wicks and sat down among the lamps to wait for footsteps on the stairs.

sections.heading: III. A Hundred Lamps
paragraphs: Someone came at midnight.
Oda Kurogane walked into the hall alone, sword drawn, river water still running out of his armour. He looked at the hundred small flames, and at the one monk kneeling among them with open hands.
“What are these?”
“One for each of them,” said Genkai. “They burn until each one comes home.”
Kurogane looked at the lamps a long time. Then he asked something Genkai didn’t understand.
“Which one of them was arguing?”

Genkai said nothing. Kurogane took the Book of the Robe from the altar, where every disciple wrote his own name on the day he took the robe, as if the answer might be inside. By morning his army had gone back across the river. It never crossed again.

Genkai could have stopped him. He had taught a hundred men how. He knelt among the lamps and let a stranger carry their names away, because he had been ordered to keep the lamps lit, and because he was afraid. He has never worked out which. That is the part he has not forgiven.

The river kept the hundred. Nobody came up the steps to blow out a lamp, so Genkai kept them lit, for forty years. The people of Ume, who did not go hungry that winter or any winter after, carried oil up the steps each month. Their children asked for lessons. He turned every one away. The open hand had cost enough.

He never wrote the names down again. That seemed like something only a man who expected to forget would do. He had the beads. Every night he told them over, a name for each, and finished on the little fist.
The winter he turned eighty, he came to a smooth round bead and could not find its name.
He sat with it until the lamps needed oil. He could see a face, and careful hands. The name would not come.
In the morning he wrapped his hands and walked down the hundred steps toward the river.

sections.heading: IV. Sixty Guards
paragraphs: Kurogane had been dead six years. His son, Oda Yorikane, held the castle across the river with sixty men. The first met Genkai at the outer gate: a boy of nineteen or so, holding his spear too close to the point.
“Go home, grandfather,” he said, not unkindly. “There are sixty of us. You’ll die here.”
Genkai looked at him and thought of a bridge, and a hundred young men who had been told the same thing and walked onto it anyway.
“I have outlived braver men,” he said. “Come.”
He did not hurry. The spear came, and he turned it with the flat of his palm, stepped inside, and laid his hand on the boy’s chest. The boy sat down. So did the next man, and the next.

It took most of the morning, and he could not stop teaching. “Your weight’s on your heels.” “Don’t watch my hands. Watch my hips.” A sergeant he sat down three times said, “Thank you, Master,” before he could stop himself.
Nobody died. One man broke his wrist falling down the keep stairs, and Genkai stopped to set it.
By the great hall, half the garrison was trailing after him, rubbing their chests. When he knelt before the young lord, they sat down along the walls like students.
Yorikane was perhaps thirty, with an undrawn sword across his knees.
“I’ve come for a book,” Genkai said. “It has a hundred names in it. That’s all I want.”
“I know the book.” When it was brought, its cover bore a stain the shape of a wet hand. “My father kept it by his bed. He was looking for one name.”
“He asked me which one was arguing.”

“He told me. That afternoon he went onto the bridge himself, and a young monk put him on his back with a knee on his chest. My father saw the fist come up. He knew the look of a man deciding. Then the boy opened his hand, slapped the planks beside my father’s head, and shouted up at the mountain, ‘Fine! You were right!’ And threw him in the river.”
Yorikane turned the book over. “My father climbed out and called up the archers. He never spared himself that part. He said the boy shouted as if somebody up there was keeping score.”
“Somebody was,” said Genkai.

He opened the book. ISAMU, in a hand that had pressed so hard it tore the paper. Two pages on, small and careful, was the name that went with the round bead: Sōta, who had carved his bead four times to get it round.
Genkai held the book to his chest. For a long while nobody spoke.
“Who teaches it now?” Yorikane asked at last.
“Nobody.”
“Then my father killed a hundred and one of you at Ume,” said the young lord. “It just took the last one forty years.”

sections.heading: V. The Last Teacher
paragraphs: Genkai carried the book home and spent the winter on the steps with a chisel. A hundred steps, one name each, from the river road to the temple gate, so that anyone who climbs to Kōzan is carried up by them. Sōta is near the top, where it is quiet. Isamu is on the bottom step, where everyone has to deal with him first.
When it was done, he sat on that step and kept his half of the bargain.
“You were right,” he said. He didn’t say about what. Isamu had promised to decide on the way up.
The children of Ume tend the lamps now, all hundred and one. The last is his. He intends to come home and blow it out himself.

In the duelling rings they call him the Last Teacher. He is an old man with heavy white brows and a string of a hundred plum-wood beads, one of them a fist. He wraps his hands so tightly across the knuckles that he could not make a proper fist if he tried. He has no intention of trying.

He fights the way he taught. He waits. He turns blades aside with the flat of his palm, steps inside them, and takes away whatever his opponent is standing on: footing, guard, certainty. Then they sit down. He has never killed anyone in a ring.
Young fighters like to tell him what they will do to him. He listens the way he used to listen to Isamu. Then he says, “I have outlived braver men. Come.”
He means both halves. A hundred braver men went down to the bridge at Ume while he stayed with the lamps. And at Kōzan, every first lesson began with that last word.

He came to the rings because that is where the young go who think a fist is quicker. After every bout he corrects one thing and offers an open hand to help the beaten fighter up. Most take it. He is waiting for the one who knocks it away, gets up on his own, and argues.
Every disciple of Kōzan carves one bead for his teacher. There is room on the string for one more. Genkai hopes it will be badly made. He hopes it will be a fist.

quote: I have outlived braver men. Come.
